static.title: Where on the Sun is a spot?
static.note: Fourteen daily pictures of the Sun in May 2024. Move the crosshair with the two sliders onto a spot, then read its heliographic latitude and longitude and how uncertain they are. The rings marked G1 and G3 are the author’s marks of two groups, made by a stated rule: nobody else has marked these pictures. They are browse pictures, made to be looked at, so a position read here is a labeled instructional measurement, not astrometry.

controls.label: The author’s marks of G1 and G3

samples.label: The picture
samples.value: The Sun on 4 May 2024 in a browse picture from the continuum camera of NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), north up and east left: an orange disc with dark spots. The detector of this page reads 7 separate dark clusters of at least 12 pixels in it. These are clusters, not NOAA’s numbered regions, which were not retrieved.

Los círculos marcados G1 y G3 son las marcas del autor de dos grupos, hechas con una regla declarada: nadie más ha marcado estas imágenes. static.title: How fast does the Sun turn at this latitude?
static.note: The author’s marks of one spot group over the days chosen, as longitude against time with the straight line that fits them. The rate is the line’s slope; adding the Earth’s own motion gives the Sun’s rotation against the stars. Beside it, the reference law of Howard, Harvey and Forgach (1990): its form is fixed and it was not refit here. The other two modes use both groups and fit only the equatorial term, or try all three coefficients.
